description_full: Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. operates as an interior design company, and manufacturer and retailer of home furnishings in the United States and internationally. The company operates through two segments: Wholesale and Retail. It offers case goods items, such as beds, dressers, armoires, tables, chairs, buffets, entertainment units, home office furniture, and wooden accents; upholstery comprising fabric-covered items, such as sleepers, recliners and other motion furniture, chairs, ottomans, custom pillows, sofas, loveseats, cut fabrics, and leather; and window treatments and drapery hardware, wall decors, florals, lighting, clocks, mattresses, bedspreads, throws, pillows, decorative accents, area rugs, flooring, wall coverings, and outdoor furnishings. The company also sells third-party furniture protection plans and sales less prompt payment discounts, sales allowances and other incentives. It markets and sells its products under the Ethan Allen brand through design centers, independent retailers, and other third parties as well as through ethanallen.com website. Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. was founded in 1932 and is headquartered in Danbury, Connecticut.

Stock-based compensation of $404 per employee reflects an ownership culture. Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Ethan Allen Interiors Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $381M market cap on $579M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and -3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 16% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $41M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.32× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 13.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 14% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.98x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 380 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 23% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 40% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.83, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.25 vs 5y 0.79), so read it loosely.
About $11.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 53% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 13% below its DCF fair value of $17.35, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 10%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $14.59 to $21.28 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 12.4 vs 17.7, EV/EBITDA 7.9 vs 10.5 and P/FCF 9.2 vs 15.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 53% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 10.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $22.00 on average, 46% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.3%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.60).
It runs a 55% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.32x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $15.7M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.7, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.9% over 3 years, -3.3% over 5 years and -3.1% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -18.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 14.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 89%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (20 sales, net $1.1M sold).
It returns 13.4% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 5.3% in dividends).
It pays out 128% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 11.4% of the float, 5.8 days to cover.
people: With about 2,988 employees, each generates about $194K of revenue, 0.5x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
